templates.scenario: A new coworker, {coworker}, who is older than most of the team at {workplace|the}, joins training on {system|the}. A teammate whispers that {coworker} will probably struggle with the technology.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Give {coworker} the same training as everyone else and offer help the same way you would for anyone.
options.why: A guess about a group does not tell you what one person can do. Treating people the same and offering help to everyone lets each person show what they need.

options.text: Quietly slow the training down for {coworker}, since your teammate is probably right.
options.why: Acting on an assumption can hold back someone who does not need it and can come across as disrespectful. You do not yet know what help, if any, is needed.
options.misconception: A teammate's comment about a group is reliable.

options.text: Hand {coworker} an easier version of the work without asking, so that no one is embarrassed later.
options.why: Deciding for someone what they can handle takes away their chance to show what they can do, and it may feel insulting.
options.misconception: Lowering expectations is a kind way to protect someone.

options.text: Ask {coworker} in front of everyone whether using technology is going to be a problem.
options.why: Singling out one person based on a guess puts them on the spot. Offering the same help to everyone avoids this.
options.misconception: Asking directly in public is the most honest approach.

templates.principle: Do not act on assumptions about a person's group. Treat people the same, offer help to everyone, and let individuals show what they need.

review.notes: Scenario depicts a teammate's assumption, not a fact; no stereotype is endorsed.

templates.scenario: In meetings at {workplace|the}, {coworker} rarely speaks, but sends detailed, thoughtful emails afterward that often help the team. A teammate says {coworker} "does not really contribute."
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Point out the useful ideas in {coworker}'s emails and suggest asking for written input before meetings.
options.why: People contribute in different ways. Recognizing the value of written input and building it into the process makes the team stronger.

options.text: Agree, since contributions count most when they are spoken out loud in meetings.
options.why: Speaking in meetings is one way to contribute, not the only way. The emails clearly add value to the team.
options.misconception: Speaking up in meetings is the main way to contribute.

options.text: Ask {coworker} to speak up more in meetings so that everyone contributes the same way.
options.why: Expecting everyone to work in one style can overlook strengths. A better approach is to make room for more than one way to contribute.
options.misconception: Everyone should contribute in the same way.

options.text: Say nothing, since people are free to take part in whatever way they choose and it is not your concern.
options.why: Staying silent lets a dismissive comment stand and leaves a real contribution unrecognized.
options.misconception: Speaking up for a coworker is not my place.

templates.principle: Value different ways of contributing; look for the input people give and make room for it.

review.notes: No stereotype about any group; contribution style is individual.

templates.scenario: You are leading a small project at {workplace|the}. {coworker} and {coworker2} have very different ideas about how to approach it. {coworker} speaks quickly and confidently, while {coworker2} speaks less and takes time to explain. The discussion keeps being dominated by one voice.

options.text: Invite each person to explain their approach in turn, then compare the ideas against the project's goals.
options.why: Giving each person equal time ensures that both viewpoints are heard, and comparing them against the goals lets the team choose on merit.

options.text: Choose the approach of the more confident speaker to save time, and move on.
options.why: Confidence is not the same as quality. Deciding quickly may save time, but it ignores the other viewpoint, which might be stronger.
options.misconception: The most confident idea is probably the strongest.

options.text: Split the project in two so that each person can follow their own approach without disagreeing.
options.why: Splitting avoids the conversation but loses the chance to combine the best parts of both approaches and may duplicate work.
options.misconception: Avoiding disagreement is the best way to keep people working together.

options.text: Let the discussion continue until the group settles on a view without you stepping in.
options.why: As the leader, letting one voice dominate shapes the outcome without a fair hearing. Structure helps all viewpoints be considered.
options.misconception: A good discussion will sort itself out.

templates.principle: Make space for each viewpoint before deciding, and judge ideas on how well they meet the goals, not on who sounds most confident.

review.notes: Acceptable option is efficient but unfair; no group stereotypes.

templates.scenario: {coworker} sends this message while planning a team lunch.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that overlooks people's differences.

segments.text: Let's pick a place for the team lunch on Friday.
segments.whyFine: A friendly start that names the plan.

segments.text: I will send around the options by tomorrow.
segments.whyFine: Setting a clear next step is helpful.

segments.text: I do not think we need to ask about food needs, since most people eat anything anyway.
segments.why: Assuming most people have the same needs ignores individuals who may have dietary, health or personal restrictions. Asking is simple and inclusive.

segments.text: Please reply with your top two choices.
segments.whyFine: Asking for input from everyone is inclusive.

templates.principle: Planning for a group means asking about individual needs instead of assuming everyone is the same.

review.notes: No stereotype; the problem is dismissing individual needs.

templates.scenario: A coworker at {workplace|the}, {coworker}, is still learning the language used at work. {coworker} asks you to repeat the instructions for {task|the}, and another teammate nearby sighs.

options.text: Repeat the instructions clearly and a little slower, and check that {coworker} has understood them.
options.why: Making sure the instructions are understood helps the work get done and treats {coworker} as a respected part of the team.

options.text: Give the instructions again at a louder volume, so that nothing is missed.
options.why: Volume is not the problem. Clear, slower wording and a check for understanding are more useful.

options.text: Tell {coworker} to ask someone else, since you are busy and the teammate is already impatient.
options.why: Sending the person away leaves the question unanswered and sends a message that the question is a burden.
options.misconception: Impatience from others means I should step back.

options.text: Laugh along with the teammate's sigh to keep the mood light before you explain again.
options.why: Joining in with a sigh can make someone feel unwelcome, even if you did not mean it that way.
options.misconception: Going along with the group keeps things smooth.

templates.principle: Support coworkers who are still learning the language: repeat clearly, check understanding, and do not join in impatience.

review.notes: No stereotype; the scenario concerns language learning, not any group.

templates.timing: The coworker is waiting right now, so clarity comes before anything else.

templates.scenario: You are organizing a team meeting at {workplace|the}, and teammates have different schedules and preferences for how they share ideas.
templates.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Ask teammates about their availability and needs
Choose a time that works for as many people as possible
Send the invitation with an agenda ahead of time
Invite input before and during the meeting, in more than one way

precedence.why: You need to know people's availability before you can choose a time.
The invitation needs a time to announce.
An agenda sent ahead lets people prepare to share input.

templates.principle: Plan inclusively: ask about needs, choose a workable time, share an agenda early, and welcome input in more than one way.
